questions.q: By what main process does haemodialysis remove waste products?
questions.explain: Solutes move down their concentration gradient from blood into dialysate. Ultrafiltration removes excess fluid.

open.q: By what main process does haemodialysis remove waste products?

questions.q: Which drug is commonly given in haemodialysis to prevent clotting in the circuit?
questions.explain: Heparin has a short action and can be stopped quickly.

open.q: Which drug is commonly given in haemodialysis to prevent clotting in the circuit?

questions.q: What name is given to blood and dialysate flowing in opposite directions?
questions.explain: It maintains a diffusion gradient along the whole length of the dialyser.

open.q: What name is given to blood and dialysate flowing in opposite directions?

questions.q: Give an indication for urgent dialysis.
questions.explain: Other indications are severe acidosis, uraemic pericarditis or encephalopathy, and some poisonings.

open.q: Give an indication for urgent dialysis.
open.a: Refractory hyperkalaemia, fluid overload, severe acidosis or uraemic complications

questions.q: What is the usual haemodialysis schedule for chronic kidney failure?
options: About 4 hours, three times a week
questions.explain: Intermittent haemodialysis provides solute and fluid clearance during treatment sessions, but it does not reproduce the continuous regulatory functions of healthy kidneys.

open.q: What is the usual haemodialysis schedule for chronic kidney failure?

questions.q: Which vascular access is preferred for long-term haemodialysis?
questions.explain: Joining an artery to a vein (usually radiocephalic) gives high flow and a lower infection risk.

open.q: Which vascular access is preferred for long-term haemodialysis?

questions.q: In peritoneal dialysis, what is the dialysing membrane?
questions.explain: Dialysate is run into the peritoneal cavity and drained after a dwell period.

open.q: In peritoneal dialysis, what is the dialysing membrane?

questions.q: What causes dialysis disequilibrium syndrome?
options: Rapid reduction in plasma urea and osmolality, causing cerebral oedema
questions.explain: Urea leaves the brain more slowly than plasma, so water shifts into brain cells.

open.q: What causes dialysis disequilibrium syndrome?

questions.q: What class of diuretic is mannitol?
questions.explain: It is filtered but not reabsorbed, and holds water in the tubule.

open.q: What class of diuretic is mannitol?

questions.q: What does furosemide inhibit?
options: The Na⁺–Cl⁻ cotransporter in the distal tubule
The epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct
Carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
The Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
questions.explain: It is a powerful loop diuretic that also impairs urine concentration.

open.q: What does furosemide inhibit?

questions.q: Where in the nephron do thiazide diuretics mainly act?
questions.explain: Thiazides also reduce urinary Ca²⁺ loss.

open.q: Where in the nephron do thiazide diuretics mainly act?

questions.q: How does spironolactone act as a diuretic?
options: It blocks aldosterone receptors and spares potassium
questions.explain: It acts at the collecting duct, where aldosterone drives Na⁺ reabsorption and K⁺ secretion.

open.q: How does spironolactone act as a diuretic?

questions.q: What enzyme does acetazolamide inhibit?
options: Carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
questions.explain: This reduces bicarbonate reabsorption and causes an alkaline diuresis with metabolic acidosis.

open.q: What enzyme does acetazolamide inhibit?

questions.q: Which diuretic class can cause hyperkalaemia?
questions.explain: Loop and thiazide diuretics instead cause hypokalaemia.

open.q: Which diuretic class can cause hyperkalaemia?

questions.q: What mechanism causes water diuresis after drinking a large volume of water?
questions.explain: Plasma osmolality falls, ADH release stops and the collecting duct becomes impermeable to water.

open.q: What mechanism causes water diuresis after drinking a large volume of water?

questions.q: What type of diuresis causes polyuria in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus?
questions.explain: Unreabsorbed glucose holds water in the tubules.

open.q: What type of diuresis causes polyuria in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus?

questions.q: Which of these is a thiazide or thiazide-like diuretic?
questions.explain: Examples are hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, indapamide and metolazone. They act on the distal convoluted tubule.

open.q: Name a thiazide or thiazide-like diuretic.

questions.q: Which of these is a loop diuretic?
questions.explain: Loop diuretics are furosemide, bumetanide and torsemide. They block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb.

open.q: Name a loop diuretic.

questions.q: Which of these is a potassium-sparing diuretic?
questions.explain: Examples are amiloride, triamterene, spironolactone and eplerenone. They work in the late distal tubule and collecting duct.

open.q: Name a potassium-sparing diuretic.

questions.q: How do amiloride and triamterene differ from spironolactone and eplerenone?
options: Amiloride blocks aldosterone receptors; spironolactone blocks sodium channels
Amiloride blocks ENaC; spironolactone blocks aldosterone receptors
questions.explain: Both groups reduce sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the collecting duct, so both can cause hyperkalaemia.

questions.q: Why does alcohol cause diuresis?
options: It blocks the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick limb
It stimulates ANP release from the atria
It inhibits ADH release, so less water is reabsorbed
It inhibits aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex
questions.explain: With less ADH, the collecting duct stays impermeable to water and dilute urine is passed in large volume.

open.q: Why does alcohol cause diuresis?

questions.q: What is diuresis?
options: A rise in plasma sodium concentration
A reduction in GFR from low blood pressure
A fall in urine output with water retention
An increase in urine output, usually with salt loss
questions.explain: Drugs, alcohol, excess water intake and uncontrolled diabetes can all cause it.

open.q: What is diuresis?
accept: increased excretion of water and salt

questions.q: Which diuretic classes commonly cause hypokalaemia?
questions.explain: They increase sodium delivery to the collecting duct, so more potassium is secreted. Potassium-sparing diuretics do the opposite.

open.q: Which diuretic classes commonly cause hypokalaemia?

questions.q: A patient with acute kidney injury has refractory hyperkalaemia, pulmonary oedema and severe metabolic acidosis despite medical treatment. Which intervention most directly corrects these life-threatening complications?
options: A thiazide diuretic as sole treatment
questions.explain: Refractory hyperkalaemia, fluid overload with pulmonary oedema and severe acidosis are major indications for urgent dialysis or another form of renal replacement therapy.

questions.q: A patient receiving high-dose furosemide develops hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Which nephron transporter is directly inhibited by furosemide?
options: Na+-K+-2Cl− cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
Na+-Cl− cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
Epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct
Na+/H+ exchanger in the proximal tubule
questions.explain: Loop diuretics such as furosemide inhibit NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, increasing sodium delivery distally and promoting potassium and hydrogen ion loss.

questions.q: A patient with hypertension is started on hydrochlorothiazide. Which electrolyte disturbance should be monitored because of its action in the distal convoluted tubule?
questions.explain: Thiazides inhibit the Na+-Cl− cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule and can increase distal sodium delivery, promoting potassium loss and hypokalaemia.

questions.q: A patient with cirrhosis and ascites is treated with spironolactone. Which molecular target does this drug antagonise?
questions.explain: Spironolactone competitively antagonises intracellular mineralocorticoid receptors in the late distal nephron, reducing aldosterone-dependent sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion.

questions.q: A patient with acute pulmonary oedema is given intravenous furosemide. In addition to increased urine output, which early haemodynamic effect can help relieve pulmonary congestion?
options: Venodilation with reduced venous return and preload
questions.explain: Intravenous loop diuretics can produce an early venodilator effect, reducing venous return and cardiac filling pressures before substantial diuresis occurs.
